bank: ESI Depth Module — narrative prompt bank v1.0
source: Student-scope rewrite of the 16 canonical EEI narrative prompts. Every prompt is answerable from a life that has not yet had a career: teams, group work, part-time supervision, student organizations, athletics, family, and coursework.
rules: Selected prompts are interpretive only — they never alter a score. Exactly 3 are offered after the assessment, optional, dictation accepted, no minimum word count for voice. In Track A the unselected prompts become the term's journal queue.

prompts.text: A decision in the last year where your first read turned out to be wrong or incomplete: what caused the misread, how you found out, and what it showed you about how your mind works when you do not have the full picture.

A time you held a position nobody around you agreed with and kept it: your reasoning, what the pressure to drop it felt like, how you engaged the people who disagreed, and how it ended. If you changed your mind, what changed it.
The conditions under which you are at your worst as a leader — the specific triggers and pressure points — and how you notice it early enough to do something about it.

A team you are on now: who on it is better than they are being used for and what you are doing about it, and an honest read on whoever is contributing least — is it them, the role they were given, your leadership, or how the team is set up?

The hardest conversation you have had with a teammate, employee, or friend in the past year: what made it hard, how you prepared, how it actually went versus how you expected it to go, and what you would do differently.

How the people around you push back on you. Describe a specific recent time someone challenged you directly, exactly how you responded in the moment, and what that says about what you have made it safe to say to you.
How you actually spend your time and attention in a typical week — and what you deliberately do not do. What did you stop doing in the last year, and what criteria did you use to decide?
A change you led that people did not want: the resistance you hit, how you handled it, what worked and what did not, and what you would do differently with the same group.
A time you had to get people who did not answer to you moving in the same direction: their competing interests, how you created alignment without authority, and where it broke down.

A situation where the signals genuinely pointed in different directions and the stakes were real: how you made sense of it, what your process was, what you decided, and how you judge whether your reasoning was good — separately from whether it worked out.

How a group you are part of actually makes its important decisions — not how it is supposed to. Who is really in the room, who has influence without a title, where accountability actually sits, and what you would change.
A real ethical difficulty with actual consequences — not a hypothetical. What was at stake, what you did, what it cost you, and whether you would decide the same way again.
A time people needed you while you were already at your own limit: what happened, how you functioned, and what you learned about your floor and your ceiling under pressure.

The biggest commitment you have made ahead of knowing it would work — a major, a team, a path, a project. What has to be true for it to pay off, how you are testing that, and what would make you change course.

The most significant thing you believed about leadership two years ago that you no longer believe. What changed it, what you had to give up to change it, and whether any part of the old belief still pulls at you.

How you are actually using AI in your own work right now: where you are curious, where you are resistant, where you think it makes you worse rather than better, and where you believe the human judgment still has to be yours.
